# MeTTa in TypeScript

> The engine runs inside your Node process, on a WebAssembly SWI-Prolog. No
> system SWI, no Python, no separate server. This file is how to USE the seat;
> the repository root's llms.txt covers the language and every other surface.

## Install

```sh
npm ci --prefix extensions/node
```

That fetches swipl-wasm and builds the TypeScript, the browser bundle and the
engine copy the package mounts, through the package's own `prepare` script, so
a checkout that has run it carries dist/, browser/ and _runtime/. Node 22.18 or
newer, which is what package.json declares. `prepare` rather than `prepack`
because it is the one script npm's directory fetcher runs, so
`npm install file:/path/to/extensions/node` gets a package with the engine in
it.

## First call

```ts
import { metta, S, V, fn } from "./extensions/node/src/index.ts";

const m = await metta();
await m.eval(fn.add(1, 2)).one();     // 3
```

## Building terms

`S` makes symbols and expressions, `V` makes variables, `fn` names the
engine's own operations. A call on `S` is an expression with that head, and
the head is exactly the symbol you wrote:

```ts
S.parent(S.alice, S.bob)      // (parent alice bob)
V.x                           // $x
fn.add(1, 2)                  // (+ 1 2), which reduces to 3
S.add(1, 2)                   // (add 1 2), a term with no meaning attached
```

That last pair is the one to get right. `fn` maps a readable name onto the
operation the engine actually has, so `fn.add` is `+`; `S.add` builds a term
headed by the symbol `add`, which nothing defines, so it comes back unreduced.

## Asking, lazily

An answer set is a thenable and nothing runs until you await it:

```ts
const ans   = m.match(S.parent(V.x, S.bob));   // nothing has run yet
const rows  = await ans;                        // the whole answer set
const who   = await ans.one();                  // exactly one, or a refusal
const maybe = (await ans.find()) ?? S.none;     // at most one, so ?? composes
```

Abandoning an answer set stops the work: taking two rows of two thousand costs
two rows.

## Bounding and cancelling

```ts
await m.eval(term).until(AbortSignal.timeout(50));
```

## What a refusal is

The engine says which refusal it raised and this seat raises that class, so a
caller never matches the message. One class per kind the engine publishes:
`syntax` (`MettaSyntaxError.line`), `time_limit` and `inference_limit`
(`TimeLimitError.limit`, `InferenceLimitError.limit`), `restraint`
(`RestraintError.restraint`, `.limit`, `.call`), `interrupted`
(`InterruptedError`), `value` and `type` (`WireError`, `CastError`),
`assertion` (`AssertionError.operation`), `capability`
(`CapabilityError.space`, `.operation`, `.capability`), `operation`
(`OperationError.operation`, `.kind`, `.expected`, `.culprit`), `stack`
(`StackLimitError.limit`) and `source` (`SourceNotFoundError.source`); anything
else is `EngineError`. A `limit` is `undefined` where a budget expired inside a
nested query, which is the one case the engine cannot name the number. The list
is `tests/data/error-kinds.json`, shared with the Python seat.

Every refusal also carries `.ground` and `.remedy`, read off the engine's own
`(refusal ...)` catalog row for its kind and rendered by the engine with this
refusal's own fields in it: `error.remedy.title` is one line saying what to do
(`raise the bound past 0.05 seconds, or narrow the query`), `.applicability` is
rustc's (`machine`, `maybe`, `prose`) and `.edit` is the MeTTa to write, as
source text for `m.parse`. `.ground.kind` is `metta-law` or `arbiter` and
`.citation` names the place. `toJSON()` carries both, so a structured log keeps
them. `website/reference/refusals.md` is the whole table.

```ts
try { m.run("!(collapse (upto 10))"); }        // (cache upto (max-answers 2))
catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof RestraintError) console.log(e.restraint, e.limit, e.call);
}
```

## Spaces

```ts
const kb = m.space(S.kb);
```

A space can be created with restricted grants, and ordinary computation still
runs inside one that has none:

```ts
const locked = m.space(S.locked, { grants: [] });
await locked.eval(S.double(21)).one();        // 42
const reader = m.space(S.reader, { grants: ["file"] });
```

## Spaces implemented in TypeScript

The engine queries your own data. A `Map`, an array, a `Set` or a plain object
attaches as a live view in one line; anything with a shape of its own
implements `SpaceProvider` and only the methods its backend has.

```ts
const rows = new Map([["ada", 3]]);
const scores = m.attach("&scores", rows);      // live: no publication step
await scores.match(S.kv(V.who, V.n));

m.attach("&table", {
  *match(pattern) { /* yield CANDIDATES; the engine unifies */ },
  add(atom) { ... },
});
```

Capabilities are derived from the methods present, so what a provider cannot do
is refused by name. `metta-node/spaces` composes them: `union`, `readOnly`,
`overlay`, `mapped`, `diff`, `objectView`.

## Proofs, and asking the engine about itself

```ts
String(await m.why(S.quad(3)));   // the first proof, rendered
m.derivation(target);             // every proof, as a discriminated union
m.doc(S.area);                    // the (@doc ...) atom
m.solve(4, sub(V.x, 1));          // { x: 5 }: the relation, backwards
m.cast(S.Ann, S.Person);          // narrowed, or CastError naming its real types
m.forms(source);                  // every top-level form, read and not run
m.trace("!(quad 3)");             // the engine's own call and exit events
m.disassemble("dbl");             // the clauses the name compiled to
m.evalStatus(S.Point(1, 2));      // value, not-reducible or empty, for a TERM
m.reducible(S.Point(1, 2));       // false: nothing applies to that head
using _ = m.strict();             // refuse anything answered unreduced, both doors
using _ = m.limits({ inferences: 100_000 });
```

A term is as deep as the ENGINE can hold: nothing on this side recurses per
nesting level, `m.parse` answers at 500,000 deep, and past the engine's own
stack the refusal is `StackLimitError` carrying the ceiling in bytes.
`m.dispose()` releases the surface and every door refuses with `ClosedError`
afterwards, including an ask that was in flight.

## Standing queries

```ts
using watch = subscribe(kb, S.alarm(V.what), { onEvent: (e) => log(e) });
await using view = await LiveView.open(kb, S.alarm(V.what));
```

## Coordination

`race`, `merge`, `parMap`, `every`, `Channel`, `spawn`: the platform's own
concurrency, each taking an `AbortSignal`. The engine's `library(thread)` is
absent from a WebAssembly build, so this is where concurrency lives.

## The satellites

The root carries what a program reaches for. Everything else is one of 27
subpaths and costs nothing unimported: `metta-node/ambient` (a lazily booted
default engine), `/spaces`, `/structures` (`AlphaSet`, `PatternMap`,
`MatchIndex`, `ClosureView`, `TabledMap`), `/matching` (unification and alpha
keys, no engine needed), `/testing` (generators and a shrinking property
runner), `/vocabularies` (the engine's closed value sets, checked against
`&metta`), `/strategies`, `/paths`, `/parallel`, `/subscribe`, `/derivation`,
`/provider`, `/wire`, `/convert`, `/integrate`, `/algebra`, `/remote`,
`/arrays`, `/tables`, `/tokens`, `/saga`, `/lint`, `/manifest`, `/events`,
`/config`, `/random`, `/version`.

## Crossing a host type, and a value that owns its matching

```ts
import { registerType } from "metta-node/convert";
registerType(Person, {
  name: "Person",
  toAtom: (p) => [p.name, p.age],
  fromAtom: (name: string, age: number) => new Person(name, age),
});
// project(new Person("Ada", 36))  ->  (Person "Ada" 36)
```

A registration picks one of four images, and the four are the engine's own
`registry-image` vocabulary: `expression` (the default shaped form), `symbol`
(a bare name, which is how an enum reads, and it runs backwards too), `handle`
and `operations` (by reference). `autoImage(value)` is the rung beneath a
declared image and answers `"transparent"` or `"opaque"` in constant time; an
iterator is always opaque, because measuring one drains it.

A host value can also decide what it unifies with, which is Hyperon's
`CustomMatch`: give the class a `[CUSTOM_MATCH](other)` method and call
`registerCustomMatch(m.engine, TheClass)`. Registration is what turns the seam
on, so a program that does not use it carries no clause for it at all.

## Extending this seat: one declared table of points

`metta-node/seam` is this seat's extension seam, the seat-level twin of
`engine/ext_points.pl`. A point is DECLARED with a kind and its fields, a
registrant is a ROW against one, and both read back as data:
`seam.declared()`, `seam.rows()`, `seam.at(name)`. Four kinds, the engine's own
less the `host_service` split a seat has no audience for: `declaration` (every
row read), `ownership` (the first row whose `claims(...)` answers wins),
`event` (every row's `on(...)` runs), `service` (the seat writes it, a
registrant calls it). `<point>.table()`, `.claim(...)`, `.each(...)` and
`.call()` dispatch by kind and refuse the other kinds' spelling;
`.register(name, { ...fields })` refuses an undeclared point, a missing field
or an extra one by name; `.refusal(subject)` is the sentence a caller gets when
no row answers, naming the door and the registrants there are.

Points: `type`, `repr` and `reflector` keep the storage `registerType`,
`registerRepr` and `registerReflector` always used and are declared here so the
surface is one query; `provider`, `library` and `integration` are what packages
advertise under the `spaces`, `libraries` and `integrations` groups, read
UNLOADED. Services: `term`, `name`. `seam.point(name, kind, {fields, doc})`
declares one of your own. `seam.publish(surface)` writes the table into
`&metta` under `(kind extension-point ...)` and `(kind extension ...)`.

A package advertises registrations under a fourth group, `extensions`, in its
`package.json` `metta` field; `seam.advertised()` answers the names without
importing anything and `await seam.discover()` loads them. Loading is explicit
rather than on first dispatch because ESM `import()` is asynchronous; a package
that registers from its own module body needs neither call.

`metta-node/seam` is a Node-only subpath, beside `metta-node/integrate` and for
its reason: it reads a `package.json`, which a browser page has neither of.

This seat declares NO `frame` point and NO `array` point: it has no frame
notion, and its array notion is the platform's own `TypedArray` family, which
every numeric library in this runtime already produces. It names no third-party
library anywhere; `swipl-wasm` is the engine it mounts and `acorn` the parser
its `define` lowering uses.

## Integrating a library

`metta-node/integrate` wraps a module, an object or one function as operations,
installs atomically, and discovers packages that advertise themselves in their
own `package.json` under `metta.integrations`, `metta.spaces` or
`metta.libraries`. `entryPoints(group)` answers advertised names without
importing anything; `discover()` returns integrations in install order and
refuses a requirement cycle. `installReflectionOps(m)` adds `(js-attr $o $n)`
and the two-mode relation `(js-field $o $n)`, which answers a `(name value)`
pair whether the name arrives bound or unbound.

## What a space declares, and a notation of your own

`kb.handles(pattern, "Exact" | "Partial" | "Sound" | "Refuse")` declares how
faithfully a space answers one query shape, keyed by shape so a second adds a
row and routing takes the most specific. `kb.covers(effect)`, `kb.writes(atomicity)`
and `kb.emits(policy)` are keyed by space and REPLACE. `kb.digest()` is a sha256
of the content, order-independent and refused for a space holding a live host
reference. `kb.transaction(term)` runs one term atomically; the body is a term
rather than a callable because `engine_yield/1` cannot unwind through a
transaction, which is the engine's own words for it.

`registerToken(m.engine, /#[0-9a-f]{6}/, (lexeme) => G(...))` extends the
READER: the constructor gets the complete lexeme and the callable never leaves
the host. Needs `library(pcre)`, which `m.engine.capabilities()` reports.

## Reactions, and undoing what already committed

`kb.reacts(pattern, operation, {priority})` declares a rule the ENGINE runs
when a matching atom lands, under the match's bindings; the managed heads are
`insert`, `retract` and `revise`. `kb.agenda(policy)` picks which of several
fires first, from a production system's own conflict-resolution vocabulary:
declaration, recency, specificity, priority, user.

`saga(m, receiptSpace)` is the compensating-transaction journal. Declare
`compensates(m, "charge", "refund")`, run steps with `await book.run(term)`,
and `await book.rollback()` undoes them in reverse. A receipt is an ordinary
`(did op args result)` atom. A failed step commits none; rollback preflights
every compensation before undoing anything; a failed compensation keeps its
suffix so a retry resumes. The step is not itself atomic here, because
`engine_yield/1` cannot unwind through a transaction, which leaves the
classical saga [source: Garcia-Molina and Salem, SIGMOD 1987].

## What a definition says about itself

`definitionFacts(m, fn)` lowers a function's body to find out what it reaches
and throws the term away, so nothing is installed. It answers the free names,
the source span, a block comment, the join over the effects the engine
declares, and `unresolved` for the heads it declares none for. `pure` is
conservative: a body reaching an unresolved head is never called pure.

## The command line

```sh
npx metta-node run program.metta
npx metta-node eval "(+ 1 2)"
npx metta-node why "(quad 3)"
npx metta-node repl
```

## In a browser

`browser/` and `_runtime/` are what a page serves. `metta({ root })` points at
the `_runtime/` directory; a browser fetches three files out of it,
`runtime.json` and the two `wasm/` assets, and reads the engine and library
sources out of the manifest rather than as files. The documentation site is the
worked example: `website/scripts/bundle-browser.mjs` copies the kit into
`website/public/metta/` and `website/public/metta/worker.js` boots one engine
per page in a Web Worker, which is where a synchronous `run` belongs.

Two things a browser meets that a Node process does not. `loadFile`,
`libraryPath`, `mount` and `lintFile` read host paths and refuse with
`ERR_METTA_UNSUPPORTED`; `run`, `load` and `lint` take source text. And a call
to a door the standard library DECLARES while this build implements nothing for
it answers ITSELF: `!(py-atom "1 + 1")` answers `(py-atom "1 + 1")` where there
is no Python seat. `lint`'s `unimplemented-head` rule names that before it
runs, and it is the rule to run before handing a program to a browser engine.

## Where to read next

- `extensions/node/README.md` is the full surface with worked examples.
- `extensions/node/examples/` are runnable programs.
- The site publishes the same README at `/extensions/node`.
